# Exercise 1. 

People with certain kinds of stomach illness may be referred to a specialist
who will identify whether or not the cause of the illness is gastric cancer. Amongst those
referred to the specialist, the diagnosis of cancer is made in 0.7% of cases. The specialist
sees about 150 patients per month. Calculate the probability that, in a given month, the
specialist will diagnose: (i) no cases of cancer; (ii) more than two cases of cancer. Use two
methods, exact via a binomial distribution and approximate via a Poisson approximation.

## Response

The specialist sees about 150 patients per month and a diagnosis of cancer is made
in about 0.07% of cases.

This is like flipping a very biased ($p = 0.007$) coin 150 times...

The probability of no cases of cancer E(X = 0). This is the same as the probability 
of getting 0 heads in 150 flips of a biased coin with $p = 0.007$...

$$E[X=0] = (1-0.007)^{150} = 0.993^{150} = 0.349$$

So the probability of no cases of cancer is about 0.349.

Using the Binomial distribution...

```{r}
n <- 150
p <- 0.007
x <- 0
prob <- dbinom(x, n, p)
prob
```

The probability of more than 2 cases of cancer is the same as the probability of getting
more than 2 heads in 150 flips of a biased coin with $p = 0.007$...


\begin{align*}
E[X>2] &= 1 - E[X \leq 2] \\ 
& = 1 - (E[X=0] + E[X=1] + E[X=2]) \\
& = 1 - (0.993^{150} + 150 * 0.007*0.993^{149} + \frac{150*149}{2}*0.007^2*0.993^{148}) \\
\end{align*}

Again, using the Binomial distribution...

```{r}
x <- 0:2
prob <- 1 - sum(dbinom(x, n, p))
prob
```


Now approximating using the Poisson distribution, we have $\lambda = np = 150*0.007 = 1.05$.

```{r}
lambda <- n*p
x <- 0
prob <- dpois(x, lambda)
prob
```

```{r}
x <- 0:2
prob <- 1 - sum(dpois(x, lambda))
prob
```

# Exercise 2. 

According to the publishers of an encyclopedia, their quality process guarantees 
that the probability that any given page contains a typo is 0.05%. The total
number of pages in all volumes of the encyclopedia is 32 625. Calculate the 
probability
that at least 14 pages of the encyclopedia contain typos.

## Response

Using a Binomial distribution...

```{r}
n <- 32625
p <- 0.0005
x <- 14
prob <- 1 - pbinom(x-1, n, p)
prob
```

Using a Poisson approximation...

```{r}
lambda <- n*p
x <- 14
prob <- 1 - ppois(x-1, lambda)
prob
```

# Exercise 3. 

The concentration of ozone at midday at a sampling site can be assumed to
have the normal distribution with mean 12 ppm and standard deviation 3 ppm.

1.  Calculate the probability that the ozone level will be 
(i) less than 10 ppm; 
(ii) less than 14 ppm; 
(iii) less than 16 ppm; 
(iv) greater than 10 ppm; 
(v) greater than 9 ppm; 
(vi) between 9 and 11 ppm; 
(vii) between 11 and 14 ppm.
2.  Calculate the first quartile and the 95th percentile concentration of ozone.

## Response

The R function `pnorm` can be used to calculate the cumulative probabilities for a 
normal distribution.

```{r}
mu <- 12
sigma <- 3
# (i) less than 10 ppm
pnorm(10, mu, sigma)
# (ii) less than 14 ppm
pnorm(14, mu, sigma)
# (iii) less than 16 ppm
pnorm(16, mu, sigma)
# (iv) greater than 10 ppm
1 - pnorm(10, mu, sigma)
# (v) greater than 9 ppm
1 - pnorm(9, mu, sigma)
# (vi) between 9 and 11 ppm
pnorm(11, mu, sigma) - pnorm(9, mu, sigma)
# (vii) between 11 and 14 ppm
pnorm(14, mu, sigma) - pnorm(11, mu, sigma)
```

The first quartile and the 95th percentile can be calculated using the 
R function `qnorm`.

```{r}
# first quartile
qnorm(0.25, mu, sigma)
# 95th percentile
qnorm(0.95, mu, sigma)
```

# Exercise 4. 

The life span of a shrub planted to slow down erosion on exposed slopes is
modelled by a normal distribution with mean 6 years and standard deviation 2 years.
a) What percentage of the shrubs planted on a hillside would live (i) 8 years or less;
(ii) longer than 8 years; (iii) between 6 and 8 years; (iv) less than 0 years.
b) Calculate the life spans exceeded by 25% and by 75% of the shrub population.

## Response

```{r}
mu <- 6
sigma <- 2
# (i) 8 years or less
pnorm(8, mu, sigma)
# (ii) longer than 8 years
1 - pnorm(8, mu, sigma)
# (iii) between 6 and 8 years
pnorm(8, mu, sigma) - pnorm(6, mu, sigma)
# (iv) less than 0 years
pnorm(0, mu, sigma)
```

```{r}
# life spans exceeded by 25% and by 75% of the shrub population
mu <- 6
sigma <- 2
qnorm(0.25, mu, sigma, FALSE)
qnorm(0.75, mu, sigma, FALSE)
```

```{r}
mu <- 6
sigma <- 2
x <- seq(0, 12, length.out = 100)
y <- dnorm(x, mu, sigma)
plot(x, y, type = "l", col = "blue", lty = 1, lwd = 2)
abline(v = qnorm(0.25, 6, 2, FALSE), col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = qnorm(0.75, 6, 2, FALSE), col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

# Exercise 5. 

The scores from an admission test are normally distributed with mean 450
and standard deviation 100.

1. What percentage of people taking the test score between 400 and 500?

2. If a particular university does not admit anyone scoring below 480, what percentage
of those taking the test would be acceptable to the university?

3. What score is required to be in the top 10% of those taking the test?

4. A random group of 20 people takes the test in one room.

    1. What is the mean and the standard deviation of their average score?

    2. What is the probability that their average score is 480 or more?

    3. What is the probability that all of them will score below 480?

    4. What is the probability that at least one of them will score below 480?

## Response

```{r}
mu <- 450
sigma <- 100
# 1. percentage of people scoring between 400 and 500
pnorm(500, mu, sigma) - pnorm(400, mu, sigma)

# 2. percentage of people scoring 480 or more
1 - pnorm(480, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

# 3. score required to be in the top 10%
qnorm(0.9, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

# 4. random group of 20 people
```


\begin{align*}
\bar{X}_{n} &= \frac{1}{n} \sum{X_i} \\
\text{E} \bar{X}_{n} &= \text{E}X \\
\text{Var} \left(\bar{X}_{n}\right) &= \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}(X) \\
\end{align*}

```{r}
n <- 20
# 4.1 mean and standard deviation of their average score
mu_xbar <- mu
sigma_xbar <- sigma / sqrt(n)

# The mean is given by mu_xbar and the standard deviation is given by sigma_xbar. 
# The variance is given by var_xbar = sigma_xbar^2.

mu_xbar
sigma_xbar
var_xbar <- sigma_xbar^2
var_xbar
```

```{r}
# 4.2 probability that their average score is 480 or more
1 - pnorm(480, mu_xbar, var_xbar)
```

```{r}
# 4.3 probability that all of them will score below 480
pnorm(480, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)^n
```

```{r}
# 4.4 probability that at least one of them will score below 480
1 - pnorm(480, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)^n

```

# Exercise 6. 

A machine which automatically packs potatoes into bags is known to operate
with the mean of 25 kg and the standard deviation of 0.5 kg. Assume a normal distribution
for the weights of bags.
a) What percentage of bags weigh: (i) more than 25 kg; (ii) between 24 and 26 kg?
b) A lorry is loaded with 100 such bags. What is the probability that the total weight
of the load will be between 2400 and 2600 kg?

## Response

```{r}
mu <- 25
sigma <- 0.5
var <- sigma^2
# a) (i) percentage of bags weighing more than 25 kg
1 - pnorm(25, mu, sigma)
```
```{r}
# a) (ii) percentage of bags weighing between 24 and 26 kg
pnorm(26, mu, sigma) - pnorm(24, mu, sigma)
```
```{r}
# b) lorry loaded with 100 bags
n <- 100
mu_total <- n * mu
sigma_total <- sqrt(n) * sigma
# probability that total weight is between 2400 and 2600 kg
pnorm(2600, mu_total, sigma_total) - pnorm(2400, mu_total, sigma_total)
```
